title: Dramatis Personae

teacherSummary.text: The cast list centres on the Danish court at Elsinore: King Claudius; Queen Gertrude; Hamlet, 'son to the late, and nephew to the present king'; the lord chamberlain Polonius and his children Laertes and Ophelia; Hamlet's friend Horatio; courtiers including Rosencrantz, Guildenstern and Osric; officers and soldiers; players; two gravediggers; Fortinbras, prince of Norway; and the Ghost of Hamlet's father.

context.history: Elsinore (Helsingør) was a real Danish castle (Kronborg) controlling the sound between Denmark and Sweden; English actors had performed there in the 1580s. Shakespeare's story comes from Saxo Grammaticus's Danish chronicle via Belleforest.

significance: The list shows three sons with dead fathers (Hamlet, Laertes, Fortinbras) and a court thick with courtiers and spies, the structure on which the tragedy runs.
discussionQuestions: If someone close to you remarried soon after a death in the family, how might you feel?
Where does characterization appear in this scene, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this scene connect to the book's larger concern with revenge and justice?

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Dramatis Personae develops the idea of the court of Denmark. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of characterization and setting shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Dramatis Personae (where it begins, turns and ends) and its characterization shape the reader's understanding of the court of Denmark. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Dramatis Personae suggests about the court of Denmark. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the scene's characterization and setting), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how William Shakespeare uses characterization in Dramatis Personae to complicate the reader's understanding of the court of Denmark. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Dramatis Personae within its historical and literary context and argue how the scene's treatment of the court of Denmark responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Dramatis Personae alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the scene's handling of the court of Denmark follows or bends those conventions, using the characterization as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Dramatis Personae and its treatment of the court of Denmark. State your method, show what it reveals in the scene's characterization and setting, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Dramatis Personae as evidence for a larger claim about the court of Denmark in Hamlet. Connect close reading of the scene to the whole play, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Dramatis Personae as a hinge in the play's larger treatment of the court of Denmark. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Hamlet.

segments.script: Elsinore (Helsingør) was a real Danish castle (Kronborg) controlling the sound between Denmark and Sweden; English actors had performed there in the 1580s. Shakespeare's story comes from Saxo Grammaticus's Danish chronicle via Belleforest. The list shows three sons with dead fathers (Hamlet, Laertes, Fortinbras) and a court thick with courtiers and spies, the structure on which the tragedy runs. Characterization: Hamlet is "son to the late, and nephew to the present king": his whole conflict in one line. Setting: "Scene: Denmark": a single kingdom, a court, a castle. Structure: Foils in the cast: Laertes (son to Polonius) and Fortinbras (prince of Norway) are sons with fathers to avenge, like Hamlet. Watch for the Ghost: listed last, after the attendants: the dead king haunts the bottom of the cast list and the top of the plot.

items.text: Why might Shakespeare include two other sons who have lost fathers?

items.text: What does “Dramatis Personae” suggest about the court of Denmark? State the inference and the line that supports it.

items.text: Find one example of characterization in this scene. What does it reveal that a plain statement would not?

items.answerGuidance: A defensible line of argument: The cast list announces Hamlet's problem: he belongs to two kings. Useful evidence: “Hamlet, son to the late, and nephew to the present king” (Dramatis Personae): Hamlet's divided position. On setting: "Scene: Denmark": a single kingdom, a court, a castle. Credit any position that is supported by quotation and reasoning; push one-sided answers to address the strongest counterpoint.

items.text: What causes the main turn in “Dramatis Personae”, and what effect is it likely to have on what follows?
items.lookFor: The cast list centres on the Danish court at Elsinore: King Claudius; Queen Gertrude; Hamlet, 'son to the late, and nephew to the present king'; the lord chamberlain Polonius and his children Laertes and Ophelia; Hamlet's friend Horatio; courtiers including Rosencrantz, Guildenstern and Osric;…

items.text: As the opening scene, what does “Dramatis Personae” set up that the rest of Hamlet will need?

items.answerGuidance: A defensible line of argument: The cast list announces Hamlet's problem: he belongs to two kings. Useful evidence: “Gertrude, queen of Denmark, and mother to Hamlet” (Dramatis Personae): Gertrude's two roles. On structure: Foils in the cast: Laertes (son to Polonius) and Fortinbras (prince of Norway) are sons with fathers to avenge, like Hamlet. Credit any position that is supported by quotation and reasoning; push one-sided answers to address the strongest counterpoint.

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the scene to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.
